title: Single-packet attack: eliminate network jitter for race conditions over HTTP/2
summary: Complete 20-30 HTTP/2 requests with a single TCP packet (withhold END_STREAM/final byte per request, wait ~100ms, Nagle-batch final frames after a ping warm-up). Cuts execution spread to ~1ms (vs 4ms last-byte sync), making remote race conditions as easy as local. Default in Burp Repeater 'Send group in parallel' and Turbo Intruder (engine=Engine.BURP2, concurrentConnections=1, gate/openGate). HTTP/1.1 pipelining is sequential (head-of-line blocking) - use parallel connections + last-byte sync there. HTTP/3 possible in principle, not worth building. Still the standard in 2025 writeups.

title: Race discovery methodology: benchmark, probe for clues, minimize to 2 requests
summary: Everything is multi-step: any endpoint may pass through invisible sub-states. Methodology: (1) benchmark baseline behavior with sequential requests, (2) pick high-value multi-step endpoints (email change, invites, coupons, password reset), (3) probe with 20-30 concurrent copies looking for ANY anomaly - duplicate success, different error text, second-order state changes, (4) eliminate extra requests and prove with 2. Spotting anomalies is the single most important skill.

title: Rate-limit abuse to delay requests for multi-endpoint races
summary: Multi-endpoint races need requests to start at different times but single-packet attacks sync them. Trigger a server-side delay by flooding dummy requests into the server's 'leaky bucket' rate-limit, making the delayed single-packet attack viable even where delayed execution is required.

title: 2025 API race-condition target checklist and fix-pattern triage
summary: High-yield TOCTOU targets: voucher redemption, gift-card balance deduction, refund issuance, withdrawal (100% balance), MFA enroll-vs-disable half-states, password-reset token consumption, promo signup credits, unique-name/unique-key validation. Test with 20 parallel copies of the same request; any request succeeding more than once = reportable. Triage against fix patterns: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, idempotency keys (Stripe pattern), atomic UPDATE with WHERE balance>=X, Redis SET NX mutex, act-then-check with unique constraints - if absent, the race is real.

title: Parser Discrepancy Scan: replace canned smuggling probes with header-parsing inconsistency detection
summary: Instead of testing known CL.TE/TE.CL payloads (which 2019-2024 blocklist mitigations defeat), detect whether front-end and back-end parse HTTP headers inconsistently across the proxy chain, then confirm leads manually. Built into HTTP Request Smuggler 3.0. Creates 'an avalanche of desync research leads' and earned $200k+ in two weeks via 3 CDN compromises (Akamai, Cloudflare, Netlify) exposing ~24M websites.

title: Expect-based desync attacks: 0.CL via vanilla and obfuscated Expect: 100-continue
summary: Vanilla Expect: 100-continue gives CL.0 desync on Netlify CDN; obfuscated variants (Expect :\t100-continue, whitespace inside header name) give 0.CL desyncs on GitLab and Akamai. Expect handling acts as an early-response gadget. Test with both vanilla and whitespace-obfuscated Expect headers when a desync trigger is suspected.

title: CRLF header-injection to request-splitting to RQP escalation chain
summary: Nginx proxy_pass $uri normalizes the path and decodes %0d%0a, enabling request-header injection with no RFC-breaking mutation: split one request into two, achieve RQP and steal other users' responses. Insertion points beyond the path: custom upstream headers, session cookies (payment provider case: exfiltrated credit cards + PII from a Kubernetes cluster). Injected Transfer-Encoding turns it into a CRLF-powered CL.TE desync. Escalation to a self-propagating 'desync worm'.

title: Dangling-byte technique: make Response Queue Poisoning reliable
summary: RQP normally races the front-end connection reset ('stacked-response problem'). Send the smuggled request missing its final byte (Content-Length: 1 with no body byte): the second response is only generated when the victim's request arrives, eliminating the race entirely. Effective on every method-agnostic back-end tested.

title: Novel desync triggers catalog 2025-2026: Transfer-Encoding: gzip, multipart/byteranges CL.0, Early-Data, dual matching Content-Length
summary: Confirmed-viable trigger set: HTTP/1.0 + Transfer-Encoding: gzip (CL.0, RFC 9112 6.1 'faulty framing', hit F5 Big-IP); Content-Type: multipart/byteranges; boundary=X as plain CL.0 trigger (RFC 2616 19.2 response-only content type; worked on multiple servers, 200+ sites incl. an American bank); Early-Data header without Pre-Shared-Key (Azure AGW proxied through Akamai); dual matching Content-Length headers treated as CL:0 by Citrix NetScaler. Also: Upgrade: websocket, OPTIONS *?xyz early-response gadget on Apache, Range: , and >64KB header values.

title: Shared-Parser Confusion: hit response-processing code from requests
summary: New attack concept: servers share parsing code between requests and responses, so any response-processing feature can be exploited via a request (e.g., multipart/byteranges Content-Type, Set-Cookie processed in requests). Generalizes Orange Tsai's Apache 'Confusion Attacks' across unrelated server families. Check whether the target's parser treats response-only constructs in requests; expect many follow-up attacks.

title: Response Forking: one request, two responses as a length-independent desync primitive
summary: Some servers respond to a single request with two responses (second one HTTP/0.9-style, no headers), independent of Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding disagreement. Detect via 'clean request gets two responses' anomaly rule and double-<HTML checks. Potentially enables RQP without any framing confusion; currently hypothetical in the wild - treat as a lead to hunt for.

title: Pipelining vs smuggling triage: avoid false positives before reporting
summary: Connection reuse, keep-alive and pipelining produce responses that look like smuggling. Before reporting, fingerprint connection reuse with the published Repeater test script and rule out front-end connection reuse; genuine desyncs need the trigger to persist across connections. Client-side (browser-powered) desyncs cannot use header obfuscation - the attack must be browser-sendable cross-domain.

title: AI variant amplification: turn one IDOR into a class of findings via regex strike rules
summary: Repeater Strike: AI reads a confirmed vulnerable request/response pair, generates smart regexes, and sweeps proxy history for sibling endpoints with the same behavior pattern - one finding becomes a vulnerability class. ~61 tokens per rule, no tokens at scan time. Same pattern as 1-day variant hunting: from one confirmed primitive, mine the whole surface.

title: Micro-inspiration and evaluation-first design for AI security research
summary: Blueprint: objective -> evaluation strategy -> inspiration sources -> cascade routes. Evaluation is the first concrete step (black-box trigger vs 'request gets a different response' contamination test, no expectations about the poisoned response). For ideation, feed LLMs 1-3 sentence micro-fragments from RFCs (138 RFCs -> 15k fragments -> 30k unique vectors) instead of full context - models over-anchor on long context (context contamination). Cascade: feed every proven finding back as inspiration; ask 'how can I detect similar behavior elsewhere?' and 'does the origin enable other attacks?'. Use deterministic code for validation gates, LLM only to propose trigger/payload.

title: Protocol ruler: measure front-end input transformations with the back-end header-length limit
summary: Almost every server has a header-length limit (e.g., 64,040 bytes). If a front-end transforms input, the byte sequence length changes, shifting the limit boundary. Send overlong headers with probe byte-sequences to measure which values get rewritten, dropped or Unicode/mojibake-transformed - detects value-rewriting of IP-spoofing headers and transformation-induced desyncs. Now implemented in Param Miner.

title: Web cache deception discrepancy classes: path confusion, delimiters, static-extension rules
summary: Four classes: (1) path confusion - appended segments like /account;foo.css, /account/..%2fsettings.css that the origin routes to a dynamic handler while the cache keys the extension; (2) delimiter discrepancies - ; (Tomcat matrix params jsessionid), ?, encoded newline as path terminators; (3) static-extension blanket rules - fuzz .css .js .jpg .png .gif .ico .svg .woff .map .txt .pdf and /static/ prefixes; (4) origin normalization that strips suffixes. Probe cache and origin separately; confirm with cf-cache-status HIT / x-cache / Age on second request.

title: Safe WCD confirmation: two-account proof with cache-buster hygiene
summary: Demonstrate cache deception without harming users: account A requests the candidate URL once (victim role); immediately re-request unauthenticated with a fresh client - if account A's private data comes back, the discrepancy is real. Append unique cache-buster query values while mapping behavior, drop them only for the final controlled proof. Never deliberately cache another person's live data.

title: Wildcard cache rules + encoded traversal: cache any sensitive endpoint
summary: Relaxed cache rules like /share/* cache everything under the prefix. If the CDN does not decode %2F..%2F but the origin does, /share/%2F..%2Fapi/auth/session?cachebuster=X caches the auth-token endpoint under a cacheable path - attacker reads the victim's token (ChatGPT ATO case). Whenever a broad cache rule is found, probe it with encoded path traversal to map all cacheable origin endpoints.

title: Range Cache Poisoning: RANGE responses without 206 status get cached
summary: Some servers answer Range requests with 200 instead of 206, so partial responses can be stored in caches and reassembled by the front-end - or escaped contextually via multi-range payloads (bytes=364-382, 1-2). Send multi-range requests to cacheable endpoints and check status code + whether a cached response embeds attacker-controlled ranges.

title: Client-side prototype pollution is widespread: source probing and gadget escalation
summary: ProbeTheProto measured 2,917 zero-day client-side prototype pollution sources across 2,738 of 1M websites (10 in top-1000), with 48 leading to XSS, 736 cookie manipulation, 830 URL manipulation. Sources: query/hash/URL-driven recursive merges reaching obj[key]=val. Gadget phase: find properties third-party code reads off objects without own-property definitions (innerHTML, script src, config objects) - GALA found 133 zero-day gadgets incl. Vue CVE-2024-6783 and a Meta bounty. Polluted prototype persists only per-page on client-side; server-side persists for process lifetime.

title: Server-side prototype pollution: non-destructive black-box probes
summary: Detect server-side pollution without DoS: pollute json spaces (Express pretty-print in later JSON responses), status property (obscure status code in response), Access-Control-Expose-Headers override (reflected header), OPTIONS/HEAD exclusion, __proto__ reflection no-op vs exception, non-reflected property test, OAST via --inspect/child-process sinks. Filters: constructor[prototype][x]=y, __pro__proto__to__[x]=y nesting. Escalation targets: shell/NODE_OPTIONS/child-process options for RCE.

title: OAuth 2.1 conformance checklist: PKCE, exact redirects, removed grants, DCR
freshness_note: based on draft-13 (2025-05-28); current draft is -15 (2026-03-02) - re-read before use
summary: Audit targets against OAuth 2.1 (draft-13, 2025) and RFC 9700 BCP: PKCE required for all auth-code clients and MUST be enforced iff challenge present; redirect URIs compared by exact string match (loopback port-only exception); implicit and ROPC grants absent; no bearer tokens in query strings; public-client refresh tokens sender-constrained or one-time-use; DCR per RFC 7591/7592 with complete redirect URI registration. Presence of legacy behavior (optional PKCE, prefix redirect matching, implicit grant) is a finding.

title: PKCE downgrade attacks: challenge strip and plain-mode acceptance
freshness_note: 2025-09-15; verify plain-mode removal landed in draft-15/final RFC
summary: Servers that enforce PKCE only when code_challenge is present are downgradable: attacker removes the challenge from the victim's authorization request (or rewrites method to plain and reveals the verifier), then redeems the stolen code. Test: (1) does the AS reject token requests with code_verifier when no challenge was in the auth request? (2) is code_challenge_method=plain accepted? (IETF 125 consensus: plain must be dropped entirely; MCP inherits the vulnerable language from OAuth 2.1.)

title: Audience injection: validate signed client-assertion audiences across all endpoints
summary: New attack class (2025, IEEE S&P 2026): signature-based client authentication (e.g., private_key_jwt) must be bound to the correct audience per endpoint; flawed/absent audience handling across two or more endpoints (auth, token, revocation, introspection, PAR, CIBA, Device Grant) lets an attacker redirect or impersonate clients - user impersonation and ATO. Test: replay a valid signed client assertion against sibling endpoints and observe audience acceptance.

title: DCR abuse: pseudo-protocol redirect URIs and open-registration mix-up
summary: When DCR is supported and form_post response mode accepted, registering a client with a javascript: redirect URI can turn the authorization server itself into an XSS host. Open ecosystems: attacker registers a client at the honest AS using the URI their own AS 'owns' in a victim client's redirect list, circumventing per-AS redirect-URI mix-up defenses. Also: silent-iframe code injection - PKCE/BFF stop code redemption without client credentials but attacker JS on the app origin can still run a fresh silent flow; robust pattern to test against is a server-side verifier bound in an HttpOnly pre-auth session cookie.

title: WAFFLED: WAF bypass via content-type parsing differentials
summary: Fuzz non-malicious components (header names/values, body segments) under application/json, multipart/form-data, application/xml: 1,207 confirmed bypasses across AWS WAF, Azure WAF, GCP Cloud Armor, Cloudflare, ModSecurity. Root enabler: >90% of websites accept application/x-www-form-urlencoded and multipart/form-data interchangeably, so payloads can be moved into the representation the WAF fails to parse. Defense: HTTP-Normalizer (RFC-strict request validation) kills whole bypass classes; per-vendor regex patches do not.

title: XS-Leaks still shipping: 2025 browser channel inventory and defense matrix
summary: Cross-origin script load/error events leaked response state enabling XS-Leaks (CVE-2025-5266, fixed Firefox 139/ESR 128.11, 2025-06) - proof the class is still live in 2025 browsers. Working channels: error-event oracles, frame counting via window references, CSP-based redirect detection, network timing, cache state, focus/blur navigation. Defense matrix (SoK 2022 + MDN): SameSite + COOP + site isolation is the minimal best set; Fetch-Metadata isolation (Sec-Fetch-Dest) + framing protection as fallback; no single defense covers all (cross-window attacks resist even COOP).

title: Systematic XS-Leak hunting: state-transfer model and per-browser channel re-derivation
summary: Model: attacker transfers app state into a component's state (cache, connection pool, DOM, rate-limiter), then retrieves the observable difference. Test each inclusion method (iframe, window, script, link, object) x detectable-difference pair; automated frameworks (AutoLeak: 151,776 test cases; S&P 2023: 280 observation channels in Chromium/Firefox/Safari incl. supposedly fixed leaks) outperform hand-rolled technique lists. Old technique lists must be re-derived per browser version.
